routes.description: Establish that compassion and other humane goods arise independently of religion, then show that religious doctrine, dogma, revelation, or institutional authority appropriates those goods while adding morally harmful conditions or obstructing reform.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if independently available human decency explains the admitted goods and representative doctrinal and historical cases show religion adding material harm without supplying a necessary, uniquely religious humane contribution.

motionBridge.description: Connect the motion to whether religion adds avoidable doctrinal harm to human goods that exist without it.

centralBridges.description: Establish that compassion, community, equality, and reforming concern can arise outside or prior to Christian doctrine.
Show that authoritative teachings or revelations introduce or entrench serious harms alongside claimed religious benefits.
Explain humane religious reform as movement away from specific harmful rules toward broader human compassion.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test claims of Christian humanitarian causation against prolonged conduct under Christian institutional power.
Use concrete cases such as slavery, subordination, and conquest to test proposed religious moral foundations.

routes.description: Distinguish corrupt religion from Christianity's governing sacred ideals, locate domination in a general human condition, and show how Christian anthropology and devotion supplied foundations and institutions for universal compassion, equality, and reform.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Christian doctrines provide a coherent basis and historically consequential mechanism for humane ideals that cannot be reduced to unaided tribal concern, while apparent religious harms can be distinguished from or corrected by those doctrines.

motionBridge.description: Connect the motion to Christianity's capacity to originate, ground, and extend the humane ideals used to judge religious corruption.

centralBridges.description: Locate pride, violence, and domination in humanity generally rather than treating religion as their distinctive cause.
Ground equal human worth and moral obligation in divine love, the image of God, and the incarnation.
Trace sacred ideals into practices and institutions extending protection and compassion beyond kin, status, or tribe.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show how Christianity contains standards for condemning corrupt religious power and interpreting difficult inherited practices.
Explain why moral condemnation requires a foundation stronger than present agreement or culturally contingent preference.

sections.title: The Governing Test: Prior Human Goods or Distinctive Religious Contribution
sections.rationale: This issue defines what the motion requires by testing whether acknowledged religious goods are uniquely generated by religion or are independently human goods burdened by harmful additions.

sections.title: Slavery, Abolition, and the Pace of Christian Reform
sections.rationale: Slavery supplies the debate's principal doctrinal and historical test of whether Christianity entrenched domination or furnished the anthropology and reforming trajectory that overcame it.

sections.title: Women, Family, and Christian Social Institutions
sections.rationale: The competing accounts of scripture, monogamy, and institutional change test whether Christian teaching constrained exploitation or imposed harmful subordination on women.

sections.title: Moral Grounding, Divine Love, and Equal Human Worth
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether humane judgments can stand on shared human concern alone or require the Christian account of divine goodness, love, and persons bearing sacred worth.

sections.title: Conquest Narratives, Revelation, and Religious Violence
sections.rationale: The Canaan narratives provide a concentrated test of whether revelation authorizes grave moral harm or can be interpreted within a framework that ultimately prohibits religious violence.

sections.title: Universal Compassion and Its Historical Sources
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether concern for outsiders, enemies, and the weak is an ordinary cross-cultural human capacity or a distinctively Christian ideal made socially expansive through doctrine and institutions.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Human decency precedes religion, which appropriates human compassion and hope while adding harmful doctrines, dogmas, and revelations.
moves.attributionBasis: Woodford announces the affirmative case and develops its recurring well metaphor throughout this uninterrupted opening passage.

response.rationale: This is a constructive opening move defining the affirmative account of prior human goods and religion's allegedly harmful additions; no earlier opposing target exists.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly establishes the central affirmative framing and supplies a memorable explanatory model.

precisionFindings.rationale: The well metaphor makes the proposition recoverable, but broad terms such as religion and human decency lack material scope qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical claim that humane goods are wholly human and religion merely adds poison outruns the metaphor offered as support.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The metaphor supplies a usable inference, but the bridge from independent human capacities to religion's merely appropriative role remains underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The selected evidence is primarily an illustrative analogy and does not independently establish the historical or causal generalization asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly states the route-completion theory that religion adds avoidable doctrinal harm to independently existing human goods.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its own governing account rather than engaging a sufficiently specified live opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies decency, love, compassion, and hope as already in the human well, followed by doctrine, dogma, and revelation as additions.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: The governing poison test asks whether religion can contribute something uniquely good without also introducing something bad.
moves.attributionBasis: Woodford explicitly defines his intended claim and presents a three-hurdle test before yielding the floor to Scrivener.

response.rationale: This constructive move expressly formulates the affirmative's governing poison test and burden for assessing alleged religious contributions; it has no reply target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it provides an explicit, readily usable criterion that structures much of the later exchange.

precisionFindings.rationale: The test is plainly recoverable, though the universe of religion and the threshold for introducing something bad remain insufficiently bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The test is confidently proposed as decisive without fully defending why any accompanying bad defeats every uniquely good contribution.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The criterion is clear, but it compresses the contested bridge from coexistence of harm to the conclusion that religion poisons everything.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move clearly states a falsifiable challenge, yet the selected passage does not defend why its demanding conjunction is the proper governing standard.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It expressly defines the affirmative route's motion-level completion condition and the test applied to later examples.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move proposes a test rather than characterizing a developed opposing alternative that can meaningfully be charity-tested.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says religion cannot do something uniquely good without introducing something bad and announces proposed hurdles for testing that claim.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.proposition: Christianity distinguishes self-exalting religion from outward divine blessing and contains prophetic and Christ-centered standards for criticizing corrupt religious power.
moves.attributionBasis: Scrivener's opening identifies biblical episodes and the cross as an internally Christian critique of poisonous institutional religion.

components.text: Religion merely appropriates prior human goodness while adding corrupting doctrine and institutional power.
Christianity must identify a distinct good rather than merely internal criticism of religious corruption.

response.rationale: Biblical distinctions between self-exalting religion and outward blessing directly contact the claim that doctrine only corrupts, but do not yet satisfy the separate unique-good test.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the decisive corruption premise through internal standards while leaving the unique-contribution demand unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast between corrupt religious power and internally grounded criticism is clearly stated and bounded through specific biblical roles.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents the interpretation as a considered reading and supports it with several concrete biblical contrasts rather than certainty.

charity.alternative: Religion may contain criticism while still adding the harms identified by the affirmative.
charity.decisiveQualification: Internal criticism rebuts an undifferentiated account but does not itself establish net or unique religious benefit.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The examples coherently establish that a tradition can contain standards against corrupt power, with only the broader motion consequence left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Abraham, separated royal and priestly roles, and prophetic criticism give specific support, though representativeness across Christianity is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary internal-critique bridge by identifying scriptural mechanisms for condemning corrupt religious power.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move concedes poisonous institutional religion and distinguishes it from Christianity's governing standards without denying the underlying abuses.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts inward self-exaltation with outward blessing and cites institutional separation and prophets speaking truth to power.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.proposition: Christian devotion redirected service toward neighbors understood as divine images and generated institutions and reforms opposing infanticide, pederasty, and gladiatorial violence.
moves.attributionBasis: Scrivener develops the claim in his opening through early-Christian worship, neighbor service, and several asserted historical reforms.

components.text: Identify a uniquely religious good that is not merely an independently human contribution.
Compassion and service arise prior to religion and are only appropriated by it.

response.rationale: The asserted Christian mechanism and institutional reforms directly answer the demand for a distinct contribution and contest the claim that compassion was merely appropriated.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly supplies both a claimed mechanism and concrete candidate goods, though their uniqueness remains historically contestable.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal claim and examples are clear, but phrases such as uniquely Christianity brought lack temporal and comparative scope qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Categorical uniqueness and abolition claims exceed the comparative historical support contained in the selected evidence.

charity.alternative: Christians may have expressed ordinary human compassion through religious language rather than originating it.
charity.decisiveQualification: Institutional expression can be causally important without proving that the underlying compassion or reform was uniquely Christian.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Devotion to God, service to divine images, and institutional reform form a coherent mechanism, with causal uniqueness remaining an implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The examples are specific but broad abolition and uniqueness claims lack comparative documentation or treatment of rival historical causes.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central institutional-fruits bridge through a claimed doctrinal mechanism and several humanitarian practices.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move supplies a serious causal alternative but understates the distinction between religious motivation, historical acceleration, and unique origination.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt links serving Jesus with serving neighbors and names care for exposed infants and opposition to infanticide, gladiatorial games, and pederasty.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.proposition: Religious and secular atrocities reveal pride and violence as a general human poison, while Christianity supplies standards for condemning that poison and presents Jesus as its antidote.
moves.attributionBasis: Scrivener concedes church crimes, compares them with secular terrors, and closes his opening by identifying the cross as the antidote.

components.text: Religion is the distinctive source of poison added to otherwise prior human decency.
A successful reply must show a uniquely religious good unaccompanied by religious harm.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses violence and pride as general human phenomena rather than religion-specific additions and states that this defeats the affirmative causal label.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The diagnostic response directly challenges the causal premise, but its proposed Christian antidote is asserted more than demonstrated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The human-poison thesis is recoverable, but comparisons of secular and religious killing and the meaning of antidote remain broadly scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that secular causes killed far more and that Jesus is the antidote is asserted categorically without adequate comparative warrant.

charity.alternative: Religion may intensify general human vices even if those vices also appear in secular movements.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing nonreligious atrocity defeats exclusivity but does not by itself defeat the claim of distinctive religious amplification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexamples undermine a religion-exclusive cause, but the inference from general human vice to Christianity as antidote leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Broad comparative death claims and the curative role of the cross rest largely on assertion within the selected evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly contests the motion-level affirmative causal account and supplies the opposing route's human-condition explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly recognizes the affirmative's concern with poison but weakens it toward an exclusivity claim and omits the amplification possibility.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares atrocities committed under secular ideals with religious violence, labels the poison human, and identifies the crucified Jesus as antidote.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Religious community and charity do not come free when accompanying doctrines subordinate women and impose harms on gay people.
moves.attributionBasis: After Scrivener's opening, Woodford identifies its appeals to community and charity and applies his test through an Islamic example.

components.text: Christian community and charity constitute extraordinary religious goods and institutional fruits.
Internal religious criticism distinguishes authentic blessing from corrupt religious power.
The primary poison is generally human rather than distinctively religious.

response.rationale: The reply concedes community and charity but applies the affirmative poison test by identifying accompanying doctrinal harms; it does not answer Christianity's internal critique or general-human diagnosis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive institutional-good component is contacted, but the examples shift to Islam and leave Christianity-specific causal claims only partially answered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The good-with-cost proposition is clear, though the transition from particular Islamic practices to religion generally requires an implicit scope qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples plausibly show religiously associated harms, but their general and representative force is somewhat overstated.

charity.alternative: Religious community may produce genuine goods even when some doctrines or institutions cause harm.
charity.decisiveQualification: Conceding those goods does not establish that every community bears the cited harms or that the goods are nonunique.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The concession-and-cost structure coherently applies the poison test, but the generalization across religions and cases remains insufficiently bounded.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete examples support the existence of harms, while representativeness, doctrinal attribution, and causal comparison are not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central doctrinal-harm bridge by linking valued religious community to asserted doctrinal injuries.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move explicitly acknowledges community and charity as goods before pressing their costs, though it generalizes from sharply selected cases.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes religious community and charity, then cites unequal female testimony and violence against gay people as accompanying doctrinal costs.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Community is a human good reproducible by secular communities, so religion cannot claim it as a uniquely religious contribution.
moves.attributionBasis: Woodford clarifies his definition immediately after Scrivener challenges the breadth of the claim and distinguishes good community from unique contribution.

components.text: Christian devotion generated a distinct compassion revolution and associated institutions.
Christianity supplies a distinct antidote to generally human pride and violence.

response.rationale: The existence of secular communities directly contacts uniqueness of community, but it does not address the more specific claim about Christian institutional causation or antidote.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive uniqueness component is contacted, while the distinctive devotional mechanism and historical reform examples remain substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited proposition that community exists in secular settings and is therefore not uniquely religious is plainly and stably stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest non-uniqueness claim follows from the uncontested existence of secular communities and does not require broader uncertainty language.

charity.alternative: Christianity may not uniquely create community but may uniquely shape its scope, motives, or institutions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Secular reproducibility defeats generic uniqueness, not every narrower claim of Christian form or historical influence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If secular communities instantiate the same generic good, community as such cannot be uniquely religious; the inference is direct and bounded.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The existence claim is readily supported, although no comparative evidence establishes equivalence across all relevant community functions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central prior-human-goods bridge by identifying community as independently reproducible outside religion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply correctly rejects generic exclusivity but compresses the opponent's more specific claim about devotional motivation and institutional consequences.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes good community from unique religious contribution and explicitly observes that secular communities also exist.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Centuries of Christian political dominance provided ample power to prohibit slavery, yet Christian authorities did not categorically abolish human ownership.
moves.attributionBasis: Woodford introduces fourth-century Christian control of imperial infrastructure and contrasts prolonged inaction on slavery with other reforms.

components.text: Christianity generated major humanitarian institutions and reforms from its distinctive devotion.
Christian standards can criticize corrupt religious power from within the tradition.
Christianity functions as an antidote to general human domination and violence.

response.rationale: Long Christian political control without categorical abolition directly tests claimed institutional fruits and the strength of Christianity's proposed antidote to domination.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply supplies a historically relevant counter-test, though it does not fully compare periods, authorities, or causal constraints.

precisionFindings.rationale: The institutional-delay claim is recoverable, but Christian dominion and the asserted fifteen-century opportunity require regional and temporal qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The word arguably provides some caution, though the sweeping duration and unified-capacity claim remains stronger than the evidence shown.

charity.alternative: Christian doctrine may have constrained slavery gradually despite limited capacity for immediate universal abolition.
charity.decisiveQualification: Long political dominance is probative, but institutional capacity and doctrinal influence varied across authorities and centuries.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Extended control plus capacity for other reforms creates a strong inconsistency test, with only the uniform-capacity premise materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The broad historical duration is relevant but unsupported by representative institutional detail or comparison of abolition opportunities.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary institutional-history bridge by contrasting prolonged Christian power with failure to prohibit slavery.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument seriously tests historical efficacy while leaving room through 'arguably,' yet it still treats Christian political power too uniformly.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asserts roughly fifteen centuries of Christian control over infrastructure and contrasts that capacity with failure to declare slavery categorically wrong.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.proposition: Human brutality, pride, violence, and domination precede religion rather than arising from otherwise unpoisoned human decency, and Christianity provides a basis for rejecting them.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker addresses Stephen directly and contrasts Augustine, humanity's condition, and his own appeal to Jesus and the New Testament.

components.text: Humanity supplies an unpoisoned well of decency before religion adds pride, violence, and domination.
Religion fails unless it supplies unique good without introducing any bad.
Christian political dominance had adequate capacity yet failed to prohibit slavery.

response.rationale: The reply explicitly identifies prior human brutality as defeating the clean-well premise, but it does not answer the separate institutional delay or unique-good criterion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly attacks the decisive causal premise with counterexamples and states the need for a basis capable of rejecting prior brutality.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is bounded to the priority of human brutality and clearly distinguishes preexisting vice from later religious expression.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Phrases such as seems to be appropriately qualify the historical inference while concrete ancient references support its limited force.

charity.alternative: The affirmative can affirm prior human brutality while claiming religion adds distinctive legitimating harms.
charity.decisiveQualification: Prior brutality defeats an unpoisoned baseline but not the narrower claim that doctrine can intensify or authorize harm.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Evidence of brutality predating the relevant religion directly defeats a pristine-humanity premise, while the Christian corrective remains a further claim.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Hammurabi, the Old Testament world, and a general historical reference supply relevant examples but not a representative causal comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central human-not-religious-poison bridge by locating domination and violence in humanity before religion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move effectively challenges the literal well metaphor but does not fully preserve the strongest additive-harm version of the affirmative case.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes pride, violence, and brutality as baked into humanity and invokes Hammurabi and the ancient world against the clean-well chronology.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.proposition: Christian monogamous marriage constrained elite male sexual access and aggression, thereby protecting and elevating women and children within family and social life.
moves.attributionBasis: The extended answer cites Joseph Henrich, Matthew 19, and Jesus while repeatedly asking Stephen whether the resulting constraint was good.

components.text: Religious doctrines accompanying community subordinate women and impose serious social harms.
Humane benefits are prior human goods rather than distinctively religious contributions.
A religious principle must supply a unique good without an accompanying bad.

response.rationale: The claimed effect of Christian monogamy directly contests doctrinal subordination and supplies a candidate distinctive institutional benefit, though other doctrinal harms remain unaddressed.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The response explicitly identifies a Christian rule, mechanism, and beneficiary, but does not establish uniqueness or net effects comprehensively.

precisionFindings.rationale: The mechanism is clear, while claims about elite men, women, and children need historical and comparative scope qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical protective effect is plausible but stronger than the bounded causal evidence contained in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: Christian sexual doctrine may constrain male access while also subordinating women in other respects.
charity.decisiveQualification: One protective mechanism does not resolve the overall status or effects of the broader doctrinal system.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Restricting elite male access plausibly benefits women and children, with the step from formal monogamy to broad elevation left partly implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A recognizable mechanism and historical framing are offered, but comparative prevalence, enforcement, and countereffects remain unverified.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central institutional-fruits bridge through a rule claimed to constrain exploitation and protect families.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move squarely answers one alleged harm with a benefit but treats that benefit as more dispositive than the strongest mixed-effects alternative permits.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies Christian sexual ethics as restricting elite male access and aggressive behavior for the benefit of women and children.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: A humane Christian defense of women succeeds only by retreating from explicit biblical doctrines and importing compassion not supplied by those texts.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker contrasts his own cited scriptural passages with Glen's opening motif and directly names Glen near the conclusion.

components.text: Christian doctrine protects and elevates women by constraining elite male sexual access.
Christian scripture and devotion generate compassionate institutions and practices.
Christianity contains internal standards that criticize corrupt or oppressive religious power.

response.rationale: Citing explicit restrictive texts and alleging their omission directly challenges the claimed humane doctrinal mechanism, while not addressing internal interpretive criticism as such.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply directly contrasts claimed benefits with contrary scriptural rules, but the inference that humane interpretation must be external is underdefended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The retreat thesis is clear, but scripture, compassion, and removal from the Bible are treated too uniformly across texts and interpretations.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion that humane preaching can only come from outside scripture exceeds the selected contrary-text evidence.

charity.alternative: A Christian defense may interpret restrictive passages through other scriptural themes rather than abandon scripture.
charity.decisiveQualification: Selective omission can weaken a defense, but internal canonical interpretation is not equivalent to importing wholly external compassion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Contrary passages create tension, but the inference from tension or selection to a wholly external source of compassion is unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific restrictive scriptural language supports the challenge, though no adequate comparison of texts or interpretive principles is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central reform-away-from-specifics bridge by arguing that humane defense retreats from explicit restrictive rules.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply highlights genuinely difficult texts but materially narrows the opponent's interpretive position into simple removal from scripture.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt juxtaposes a command that a woman remain quiet with Scrivener's humane preaching and alleges that the latter removes itself from explicit doctrine.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.proposition: Slavery is wrong because enslaving a person made in God's image violates humanity's divinely granted status and its vocation to exercise dominion rather than be enslaved.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer uses explicit Christian doctrines in direct response to repeated demands that Glen explain why slavery is wrong.

components.text: Christian authorities lacked or failed to articulate a categorical doctrinal basis for rejecting human ownership.
Moral opposition to domination is an independently human good appropriated by religion.
Humane Christian reform must retreat from scripture and import external compassion.

response.rationale: The image-of-God argument directly supplies a Christian doctrinal basis against slavery and identifies its asserted abolitionist use, though it does not explain the long delay.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply answers the doctrinal-basis demand explicitly but only partially contacts the historical failure and timing component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The normative inference from divine image-bearing to the wrongness of enslavement is concise, stable, and readily recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The normative claim is well matched, but the broad historical statement about arguments bringing abolition needs qualification.

charity.alternative: Image-of-God doctrine coexisted with Christian slavery and therefore did not categorically determine abolition.
charity.decisiveQualification: A doctrine can ground abolitionist reasoning without having been consistently applied or historically sufficient by itself.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If every person images God and is created for dominion rather than enslavement, the anti-slavery inference is strong and explicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The doctrinal warrant is stated, but its claimed role in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century abolition lacks specific historical support here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central sacred-human-worth bridge by deriving anti-slavery status from universal divine image-bearing.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move provides a genuine doctrinal answer without claiming that all Christians applied it consistently, though historical sufficiency is compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that enslaving God's image is analogous to enslaving God and that humans were created for dominion rather than servitude.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.proposition: Trinitarian Christianity avoids arbitrary divine command by identifying goodness with God's eternal loving life and evil with violation of the love that shapes creation.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker presents the historic Christian-Platonist answer and develops it through the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as a community of love.

components.text: Christian compassion is imported from outside scripture and doctrine rather than grounded within Christianity.
Love and compassion are wholly prior human goods merely appropriated by religion.
Christian institutions failed historically to prohibit slavery despite their power.

response.rationale: The Trinitarian account directly supplies an internal doctrinal ground for love and goodness, but it does not answer the historical application and institutional-delay challenge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The doctrinal-source component is clearly contacted, while the inference from metaphysical grounding to actual humane performance remains incomplete.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed account is recoverable, though goodness and love are identified without fully specifying their normative content or relation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents this as the Christian account and cautiously says it addresses something about the dilemma, matching the compressed warrant.

charity.alternative: Identifying God with love may rename goodness without resolving whether divine acts are independently recognizable as loving.
charity.decisiveQualification: The account avoids crude voluntarism but still needs criteria connecting divine nature, love, and disputed commands.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Eternal relational love provides a coherent third option to arbitrary command, but the identity between love and goodness is asserted rather than analyzed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Trinitarian structure supplies a theological warrant, while no independent defense establishes the key identity or its application to hard cases.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central sacred-human-worth bridge by locating goodness and love in Christianity's account of divine reality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately addresses arbitrary command through divine character while leaving the strongest epistemic and content challenge open.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies God's Trinitarian life with love and describes creation as made, shaped, and directed for love, with evil violating that love.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.proposition: Paul addressed conduct within an existing slave society while affirming equality under Christ, and Christianity's gradual, yeast-like social transformation ultimately ended the slave trade.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker identifies Ephesians 6:5, contextualizes Paul's instruction, and invokes Jesus's yeast metaphor for gradual social transformation.

components.text: Christian political dominance could have prohibited slavery but instead tolerated human ownership for centuries.
Humane reform succeeds only by moving away from explicit biblical doctrine.
Equality and reforming concern arise independently of Christian doctrine.

response.rationale: The reply directly explains biblical accommodation as gradual transformation grounded in ecclesial equality, thereby addressing both scripture and delayed abolition, though not the selectivity objection later raised.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly supplies equality, contextual accommodation, and a gradual causal mechanism, but the asserted historical exclusivity is underdefended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The church-workplace distinction and gradualism are explicit, while the claim that this alone ended the trade is insufficiently scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The assertion that this is the only process ever to end the slave trade is far stronger than the evidence provided.

charity.alternative: Pauline equality may coexist with practical accommodation that prolonged slavery rather than reliably dissolving it.
charity.decisiveQualification: A gradual trajectory is possible, but coexistence and delay require evidence that accommodation causally promoted eventual abolition.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Internal equality plus yeast-like transformation forms a plausible gradualist account, but the bridge to eventual abolition and exclusivity remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Pauline and Jesus references support an internal trajectory, while the decisive historical claim rests largely on assertion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the subsidiary institutional-history bridge by offering a doctrinal explanation for gradual rather than immediate reform.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply acknowledges existing structures rather than denying them, yet it treats the asserted gradual trajectory as historically dispositive without comparison.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes equality among brothers and sisters in Christ, accommodation within existing work structures, and Jesus's yeast metaphor for gradual transformation.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Christian gradualism cannot excuse slavery when Christian rulers made radical institutional changes elsewhere but left slavery intact until the Enlightenment era.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker directly addresses Glen, contrasts slavery with bans on crucifixion, gladiatorial combat, and infanticide, and invokes Enlightenment chronology.

components.text: Christianity necessarily transformed slavery gradually because its movement works socially like yeast.
Christian institutions achieved radical reforms such as opposition to infanticide.
Image-of-God doctrine supplied an abolitionist basis against slavery.

response.rationale: The reply expressly identifies selective willingness to make other radical changes as defeating the claimed necessity of gradualism and states the historical-delay consequence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It targets the key gradualist premise with the opponent's own infanticide example and identifies the resulting inconsistency directly.

precisionFindings.rationale: The selective-gradualism challenge is clear, though references to theocracy, the Enlightenment, and the timing of abolition need regional qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The contrast strongly challenges necessity, but suspicious timing and Enlightenment attribution exceed the support shown in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: Different reforms can face different institutional constraints, so rapid action on infanticide need not make immediate abolition feasible.
charity.decisiveQualification: The contrast defeats a bare appeal to gradualism unless those differing constraints are specifically explained.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Evidence of capacity for radical reform directly undercuts unexplained necessity of gradualism, though it does not prove identical feasibility across issues.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The internal comparison with claimed infanticide reform is probative, but timing and Enlightenment causation remain insufficiently documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary institutional-history bridge by exposing an unexplained asymmetry in Christian reform speed.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly uses the opponent's own radical-reform claim and leaves a clear route for a differentiated institutional response.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts asserted radical Christian reform of infanticide and establishment with the much later emergence of categorical opposition to slavery.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.proposition: Christianity scaled compassion beyond kin and tribe by making love of enemies and concern for outsiders and the weak culturally authoritative despite contrary evolutionary pressures.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker develops a kin-selection and group-selection contrast, then invokes Nietzsche's account of distinctively Christian concern for enemies and the weak.

components.text: Community and compassion are ordinary human goods reproducible without religion.
Compassion and love are wholly prior human goods merely claimed by religion.
Christianity must identify a uniquely religious moral contribution.

response.rationale: The reply narrows the disputed good from generic community to enemy-love and concern beyond tribe, directly addressing uniqueness and the alleged merely human source.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies a specific distinctive norm and an evolutionary contrast, though it does not establish historical uniqueness comparatively.

precisionFindings.rationale: Enemy-love and care for the weak are clear, but claims that such compassion is unnatural require biological and cross-cultural qualification.
